reasoning: The underlying statistical problem (sample size / confidence for certifying a low binary failure rate) is fully solved off-the-shelf: acceptance sampling, OC curves, and Clopper-Pearson binomial intervals are textbook quality-engineering tools, and ML reliability assurance with quantitative acceptance criteria already exists (arXiv 2112.0646). Within AI control specifically, published control evals (AI Control 2312.06942; Ctrl-Z 2504.10374) already report point estimates and some confidence intervals (e.g., 80% CIs on safety/usefulness curves), and "Notes on control evaluations for safety cases" reasons about audit budgets and estimation under rare events. However, no work frames control-eval episode-count requirements through acceptance-sampling OC curves with explicit producer/consumer risk, and the "Notes" post explicitly uses heuristic/qualitative estimation rather than formal sampling theory; crucially, no published work systematically re-analyzes existing control-eval safety scores to show their point estimates overstate the evidential support. The proposed specific angle and re-analysis are unexplored, though all the statistical building blocks are standard.

evidence.title: Notes on control evaluations for safety cases
evidence.summary: Most directly relevant. Discusses estimating P(catastrophe) under control protocols and audit budgets (e.g., auditing 0.5% of 200M tasks), but a WebFetch confirms it uses qualitative/heuristic estimation (importance sampling, extrapolation) rather than binomial confidence intervals, acceptance sampling, OC curves, or producer/consumer risk to derive required episode counts. Establishes the problem but does not solve the proposed contribution.

evidence.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
evidence.summary: Foundational control-eval paper; red team estimates max probability of safety failure under a protocol. Reports estimates of catastrophe probability but does not derive how many episodes are needed for a given confidence, nor apply acceptance-sampling/OC-curve reasoning.

evidence.title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
evidence.summary: Recent control-eval work; safety/usefulness curves reported with 80% confidence intervals, showing CIs are already used in control evals. But sample size is not derived from a target sabotage rate via OC curves/producer-consumer risk, and there is no acceptance-sampling certification framing.

evidence.title: Reliability Assessment and Safety Arguments for Machine Learning Components in System Assurance
evidence.summary: Shows ML reliability assurance already uses acceptance criteria comparing P(safety contract fulfilled) against quantitative thresholds, and rare-event sampling methods. Demonstrates the statistical certification machinery is established in ML assurance generally, though not applied to AI control sabotage rates.

evidence.title: Operating Characteristic (OC) Curve / Acceptance Sampling
evidence.summary: Confirms acceptance sampling, OC curves, and producer/consumer risk are standard textbook quality-engineering tools relating sample size and observed defectives to acceptance probability. The proposed method is off-the-shelf; novelty rests entirely on the control-eval application and re-analysis.
